h1: Nerve hydrodissection and nerve blocks in Hyderabad
summary: Nerve hydrodissection uses fluid, placed under ultrasound, to separate a trapped nerve from the tissue pressing on it, leaving the nerve itself intact. Nerve blocks are used both to treat a nerve that is firing and to prove where pain is coming from before anything else is done. At Halcyon both are done under local anaesthetic as day care, and you go home the same day.

quick_facts.label: Purpose
quick_facts.value: Free a trapped nerve, or diagnose and treat a painful one

quick_facts.label: Surgery involved
quick_facts.value: None; the nerve is left intact

sections.h2: What are nerve hydrodissection and nerve blocks?
paragraphs: Nerve hydrodissection is a non-surgical procedure in which fluid is injected under ultrasound around a trapped (entrapped) nerve to separate it from the tissue that is pressing on or sticking to it. A nerve block is an injection placed on or beside a specific nerve to calm it, or to test whether it is the source of the pain.
At Halcyon in Hyderabad these form one pathway: freeing a nerve that is squeezed, and quietening one that is firing.

Hydrodissection works by using a carefully placed volume of fluid to open up a space around a nerve that has become compressed or stuck. Healthy nerves glide as you move; when scar tissue, a thickened band or swollen tissue presses on one, it can cause pain, tingling or numbness. The fluid, usually saline and sometimes with local anaesthetic or dextrose, is watched on ultrasound as it lifts the tissue away. Relief often begins on the table.

A nerve block delivers medicine, usually a local anaesthetic and sometimes a steroid, to a precise point. Used diagnostically, a block that settles the pain is the strongest evidence available that the right structure has been found. Used as treatment, it can calm an irritated nerve so that movement and rehabilitation become possible.
At Halcyon, hydrodissection and nerve blocks are most often used for these conditions. The named procedure depends on what the scan and examination show.
bullets: Elbow, hand and wrist pain, such as carpal tunnel syndrome — nerve hydrodissection
Sciatica — a transforaminal or epidural injection placed at the irritated nerve root
Slipped disc pressing on a nerve root — an image-guided epidural injection
Shoulder pain and frozen shoulder — a suprascapular nerve block, often with hydrodilatation
Low back pain — a diagnostic or medial branch block to prove which structure is the source

sections.h2: Who they suit, and who they do not
paragraphs: Hydrodissection usually suits people with symptoms of a trapped nerve — pain, pins and needles or numbness in the area that nerve supplies — where ultrasound shows the nerve being compressed. Nerve blocks suit people whose pain source needs confirming, or whose irritated nerve needs calming so that exercise and recovery can proceed.

They are not a substitute for urgent surgical assessment when there is severe or worsening weakness, or loss of bladder or bowel control. An active infection at the site, some bleeding problems, or poorly controlled diabetes may mean the procedure is delayed or changed, so tell the team about your health and medicines when you book.
Most of these procedures are completed in a single appointment at the Kukatpally centre, and most people are home within about two hours.
bullets: The consultant takes your history and examines you, including nerve function.
The nerve or structure is scanned with diagnostic ultrasound in the same room.
If a procedure is right, the skin is cleaned and numbed with local anaesthetic.
Under live imaging, a fine needle is guided to the nerve or to the chosen level of the spine.
For hydrodissection, fluid is injected in stages to free the nerve along its course; for a block, the medicine is placed at the target.
Your symptoms are checked, which for a diagnostic block helps decide the next step.
You rest briefly, receive aftercare instructions and a review date, and go home.

paragraphs: Most people walk out after hydrodissection or a nerve block and go about a normal day. The area may feel numb or heavy for a few hours while the local anaesthetic wears off, so take care with that limb and follow the advice you are given about driving.

Note how your pain changes over the following hours and days, especially after a diagnostic block, as this guides the plan. Gentle movement is usually encouraged; a stretching, splinting or exercise programme may be suggested to keep the nerve gliding freely.

These procedures are generally well tolerated. Common effects are temporary numbness or weakness in the area supplied by the nerve, soreness and bruising at the needle site, and sometimes a short flare of symptoms. If a steroid is used, people with diabetes may notice a temporary rise in blood sugar.

Serious complications such as infection, bleeding or nerve injury are uncommon; ultrasound lets the consultant see the nerve and needle throughout. Seek urgent care for fever, spreading redness, new or worsening weakness, or loss of bladder or bowel control.

faqs.a: Nerve hydrodissection is an ultrasound-guided injection of fluid around a trapped nerve to separate it from the tissue pressing on it. The nerve is left intact and nothing is cut. It is often used for problems such as carpal tunnel syndrome, and relief often begins on the table. At Halcyon it is done under local anaesthetic as day care.

faqs.q: Can carpal tunnel syndrome be treated without surgery?
faqs.a: In many cases, yes. At Halcyon, carpal tunnel and similar wrist and elbow problems are usually treated with nerve hydrodissection or a regenerative injection rather than surgical release. Ultrasound shows where the median nerve is compressed, and fluid is used to free it. If the nerve is severely damaged or weakness is progressing, the consultant will tell you whether surgery should be considered.

faqs.q: What is a diagnostic nerve block?
faqs.a: A diagnostic nerve block is a small injection of local anaesthetic placed on one suspected structure. If the pain settles, that structure is the source and treatment follows from it; if it does not, the plan changes. In the low back and neck especially, this step is what stands between a diagnosis and a guess, and it comes before radiofrequency.

faqs.q: Is a nerve block the same as an epidural injection?
faqs.a: An epidural or transforaminal injection is one kind of nerve block, placed near the spinal nerve roots. At Halcyon it is the usual treatment for sciatica and for a slipped disc pressing on a nerve root, and it is placed under imaging at the level the scan and examination have identified, rather than across the whole area.

faqs.q: How long does a nerve block last?
faqs.a: It varies. The numbness from the local anaesthetic wears off within hours, but a treatment block can calm an irritated nerve for much longer, and some people need a repeat. How long relief lasts depends on the condition and what is causing it, and the consultant will give you a realistic answer for your case.

faqs.q: Can I drive home after a nerve block?
faqs.a: It depends on where the block is placed. A block in the leg, arm or spine can leave the limb numb or weak for a few hours, so it is safer to arrange for someone to drive you home. Ask the team when you book.

schema.how_performed: Under ultrasound or other image guidance and local anaesthetic, fluid is injected around a trapped nerve to free it, or medicine is placed on a specific nerve to diagnose or treat pain.
schema.preparation: Bring recent X-ray, MRI or scan reports and a medicine list, tell the team about blood thinners or diabetes without stopping any medicine on your own, and consider arranging someone to drive you home.
schema.followup: Note how your pain changes after the procedure, especially after a diagnostic block, and attend the review date given, where the next step is planned.
